title: Woman ‘tortured’ for taking possession of grabbed land in Sahiwal
content: SAHIWAL: A woman, who had taken possession of her inherited land after being illegally occupied for around 30 years, was allegedly abducted, tortured and humiliated by 12 armed attackers, including three women, at Chak 93/9-L. The victim, Mardan Bibi, got possession of her land she had inherited under Ghori Pal Scheme, with the help of Pera Force, police, revenue department and the district administration, following 30 years of illegal occupation. As per the First Information Report (FIR), registered under sections 50, 148, 149, 447, 511, 365, and 354 of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC) on the complaint of her son, Nomir Abbas, the attackers, armed with pistols and rifles, kidnapped Mardan Bibi, subjected her to torture, and fled on the arrival of a team of Yousafwala police, which came to rescue her. As per police sources, the land inherited by the victim had been illegally occupied by one Khudayar Baloch and others for nearly three decades. After repeated appeals by Mardan Bibi, Sahiwal Commissioner Asif Tufail ordered the revenue department, Punjab Enforcement and Regulatory Authority (Pera) Force, and district administration officials to restore possession of the land to the legal owner, Mardan Bibi. Accordingly, in an operation led by Assistant Commissioner Nouman Qasir, the land was retrieved from illegal occupants and its possession was given to the complainant. However, as soon as the officials team left the village, Khudayar Baloch, Ali, Sarfraz, Yaseen Baloch, Gulaan Bibi, Nooran, Sheenan, Allah Maafi, and their four unidentified accomplices returned with arms. The FIR says that the suspects dragged the victim by her hair, and forcibly took her away on a motorcycle, after covering her face with a piece of cloth. When her cousin Akram tried to intervene, he was injured by the suspects. However, the police, on being informed of the attack on the 15 helpline, arrived at the scene, rescued the woman and arrested six of the suspects, while others managed to escape. The police say raids are underway to apprehend the fleeing suspects. Published in Dawn, August 11th, 2026

title: NEW: Five men arrested in Mashonaland Central for raping a minor
content:
Rumbidzayi Zinyuke
FIVE men have been arrested in Mashonaland Central province after they allegedly sexually exploited a 14-year-old girl on different occasions.
The arrests followed a joint operation involving traditional leaders, the Zimbabwe Republic Police and Department of Social Development (DSD) after community members reportedly raised the alarm over a villager who was repeatedly buying contraceptives for the minor.
Chief Bushu of Shamva in Mashonaland Central said investigations revealed that the man, together with several others, had allegedly been taking turns to sexually abuse the girl.
“We found out that one man was buying contraceptives for this child and that he, together with other men in the community, was taking advantage of her and sleeping with her. The Department of Social Development brought the issue to us, and I immediately engaged the officer-in-charge (ZRP). Together, we came up with a strategy to catch these men and they were arrested,” he said.
Chief Bushu said the suspects were referred to the police because the alleged offences were criminal matters that fell outside the jurisdiction of the traditional courts.
The case was uncovered through the community-driven “Not in My Village” campaign, a community-led initiative spearheaded by the Zimbabwe Council of Chiefs, National AIDS Council with support from the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) through the Safeguard Young People (SYP) Programme and the Health Resilience Fund.
The campaign mobilises traditional leaders, parents, teachers, religious leaders, police, social welfare officers and other community structures to prevent child marriages, teenage pregnancies, sexual abuse and new HIV infections among adolescents.
Chief Bushu said when he became chief in 2018, child marriage was one of the biggest challenges facing his area and province.
“Mashonaland Central used to constitute more than 50 percent of child marriages in the country. Over the years, we have worked hard with all stakeholders in a bid to fix our community. We realised that despite our different religions and beliefs, we had to work together to tackle this challenge,” he said.
Following consultations with communities, chiefs developed common guidelines that are now being used across the province to determine which cases should be handled through traditional courts and which should be referred to the formal justice system.
To better protect survivors, Chief Bushu said traditional leaders had also established special children’s courts, where cases involving minors are heard privately to preserve their dignity.
“We created a children’s special court because we realised we could not deal with such cases together with all other matters in front of everyone. We have to maintain the children’s privacy and dignity,” he said.
He added that regular engagement between chiefs and the Judiciary, including quarterly visits by magistrates to traditional courts, had strengthened coordination and improved the handling of cases involving children.
“All the chiefs are now part of the campaign, and we think these cases are significantly going down. This is why we are here today, still fighting for our children’s rights and for them to restore their lives and go back to school,” he said.
In recent years, Mashonaland Central has recorded significant progress in reducing child marriages, teenage pregnancies and new HIV infections among young people through community-led interventions under the “Not in My Village” campaign.

title: Rethink Business Centre Management
content:
Affordable workspace is not a luxury for small businesses; it is one of the basic conditions for enterprise growth.
When rents are beyond reach, entrepreneurs stay trapped in backyards, informal stalls and survivalist activity instead of moving into spaces where they can produce, employ and compete.
The benefits are practical and immediate.
Lower rental costs free up money for tools, equipment, material and stock. Larger premises can lift productive capacity beyond what a backyard operation allows, while visibility in the right location improves access to customers.
The creation of affordable workspace as a strategy for entrepreneurs to migrate from the informal sector into the mainstream economy and to help newcomers to the business arena scale or grow their enterprises was embraced as a policy at the dawn of Namibia’s nationhood.
This resulted in the government building business incubation centres, small and medium enterprises (SME) business parks and industrial centres across the country.
Windhoek’s municipality and local authorities of larger towns embraced a similar economic growth strategy by creating open markets and SME business hubs.
That is why the neglected state of public enterprise facilities across Namibia should trouble every taxpayer. These centres were not built as monuments to policy ambition; they were meant to become practical stepping stones for Namibians trying to build livelihoods.
It is no better in other towns, but working at Keetmanshoop last week, it was soul-destroying to see four such centres, all built with taxpayer money, either closed, idle, dysfunctional or operating far below their intended purpose.
Interaction with local entrepreneurs revealed possible causes of this sad situation: political infighting, absence of coordination between public sector entities, poor property management, favoritism coupled with dubious tenant selection, officials who do not have the skills nor the ability to run a business centre or industrial property, among others.
Apparently, those properties that cost million dollars to built and due to the lack of maintenance are now in a perilous state.
This is not about creating a handout culture. It is about giving aspiring entrepreneurs a realistic path from informal trading into formal business and giving emerging enterprises the space they need to grow.
At times challenges appear insurmountable yet solutions stare us in the face. Here is something to think about.
Bureaucrats seemingly often have a fixation on the mobilisation of foreign direct investment (FDI) and tend to ignore that an economy grown from the bottom up assures viability in the short term and sustainability eventually.
As for resource allocation, entrepreneurial driven economic growth funding then goes to FDI attraction.
Costly investment promotion missions are embarked upon with lengthy stays abroad, sometimes spanning six months’ stays in costly accommodation attending world trade fairs.
The result nearly always are promises of billions of dollars of FDI yet the reality on the ground reflects a different picture.
FDI has an important economic developmental role but so does grassroots enterprise development.
Existing workspace must be managed better and resources allocated to develop more affordable workspaces.
Is it not time to rethink structures in place that are failing to deliver on their mandate and to create devolved government entities, overseen by regional government administrations, to operate and manage business incubation centres, SME business parks and industrial centres across the country properly?
- Danny Meyer is reachable at danny@smecompete.com

title: Dozens of greyhounds to land in Australia as NZ racing ban begins
content:
Charter flights to bring about 150 greyhounds to Australia as NZ racing ban begins
Sat 1 Aug 2026 at 2:48pm
In short:
A ban on greyhound racing came into effect in New Zealand today.
Greyhound Racing New Zealand has organised charter flights to export about 150 dogs to Australia for trainers to continue racing.
What's next?
It is estimated 1,400 greyhounds will retire from the sport and be rehomed in New Zealand.
Chartered flights will ferry up to 150 greyhounds to Australia as trainers pivot from a racing ban coming into effect in New Zealand.
The ban, which was first announced in December 2024 and legislated in April this year, took effect on Saturday after years of animal welfare concerns.
Ten greyhounds were euthanised during New Zealand's final racing season, including one days before the ban began.
Heather Simpson, the Greyhound Transition Agency (GTA) head, said she was aware that Greyhound Racing New Zealand had organised charter flights for about 150 dogs to go to Australia to continue racing.
"There is nothing in the legislation that stops trainers choosing to export their dogs to Australia; some of these dogs actually will be partly owned by Australians," she told Radio New Zealand.
Greyhound racing remains legal in most Australian jurisdictions, banned only in the Australian Capital Territory.
Plans for an industry phase-out in Tasmania have stalled after the government pulled a bill from the upper house in April when it appeared not to have enough support to pass.
Word of the chartered flights first emerged through a leaked message from a private greyhound racing group, Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi told a Senate Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport Legislation Committee hearing in April.
She said the move appeared "to be kind of a deliberate attempt to avoid" New Zealand's transition agency.
"If they survive, they will become the responsibility of Australians to rehome," she said.
"And you would know we're already in a rehoming crisis."
Brant Smith, a senior biosecurity executive at the Department of Agriculture and Fisheries, told the senate hearing the government had been working with New Zealand's Ministry for Primary Industries on the dogs' import.
He said they would be classed as "companion animals", but may be used for racing once in the country.
"As to how they are then used, that's not something that we have control over thereafter because they're being imported as companion animals like other animals … and this is not unusual," he said.
Mr Smith said a similar contingent of greyhounds was imported to Australia in April 2025.
"In the previous consignment, I think approximately 80 came similarly, and they were just imported under our normal conditions," he said.
It is estimated a further 1,400 dogs will remain in New Zealand and require rehoming by the GTA.
Ms Simpson said the rehomed dogs would be regularly checked under a welfare program.

title: Children’s helpline says number of calls about child domestic abuse cases has risen 80% in five years
content:
Children’s helpline says number of calls about child domestic abuse cases has risen 80% in five years
The charity received 8,488 reports in the last year compared to 4,599 in 2021-2022
- Bookmark
A children’s charity has seen an 80 per cent increase in reports of concern for a child experiencing domestic abuse in the last five years.
The NSPCC received 4,599 contacts with the primary concern being domestic abuse in 2021-2022, with this rising to 8,448 in 2025-2026.
Almost a third of these cases resulted in a referral to local agencies such as police forces and children’s social services.
One person who called the NSPCC Helpline said: “My sister recently left an abusive situation with her six-month-old baby, but her ex-partner is still in control of their finances and emotionally abusing her.
“Her ex has drained their accounts so she can’t buy what she needs for my niece.
“The ex is bombarding her with threats online and via text, even saying they will kill themselves if she doesn’t go back or let them see the baby. Where can we get support and protection for my sister and niece?”
Domestic abuse can include coercive control as well as emotional, verbal, physical and financial abuse.
Witnessing abuse can have a lasting impact on a child’s mental health, with signs including aggression, bed-wetting, attention seeking, tantrums, anti-social behaviour, withdrawal and problems in school.
Margaret* suffered years of abuse at the hands of her ex-husband. She said: “I had always known Tony* was controlling, but after our wedding he became emotionally and psychologically abusive, threatening me and belittling me all the time. Then he started being physically abusive.
“We had two children and he became abusive towards them too, shouting and beating them with belts and shoes when I wasn’t there. I could see that they were really affected. They were subdued, sullen and didn’t really behave like children at all.
“One day, I finally snapped and called the police. They helped get us to a safe house.
“I was really worried about whether my children would be able to get over the abuse they had witnessed and endured. They took part in the NSPCC’s domestic abuse programme, and the light has come back into their eyes. They changed from quiet and subdued children to boisterous and playful – like they’ve released whatever they’d been holding on to.
“If there are any parents reading this and going through something like us, or you know someone who is, help is out there. I know my children will be OK, but without help, they may not have been.”
Paddi Vint, NSPCC Helpline Service Head, says: “It’s alarming that we are seeing record levels of adults contacting our Helpline about a child experiencing domestic abuse.
"Domestic abuse is often hidden, with stigma and shame making it harder to ask for help. Children and young people might also feel frightened and confused, keeping the abuse to themselves.
“If you’re worried about a child, you can speak to our free NSPCC Helpline in complete confidence. Reaching out can be the first step to help families begin to move forward.”
If you are a child and you need help because something has happened to you, you can call Childline free of charge on 0800 1111. You can also call the NSPCC if you are an adult and you are worried about a child, on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adults on 0808 801 0331
*Names have been changed to protect identities

title: Celebrated at birth, pushed into sex work
content:
Identities of all sex workers, former sex workers, and their families have been changed to maintain privacy
Sitting in her older daughter’s room, where one corner is covered with maps and math formula sheets, Savitri, a 40-year-old former sex worker, recalls when she began hating her profession. “It was when my girls turned five and seven,” she says. “I had decided that my daughters would never live the life I had. They would live with dignity.”
Although she continued in the profession for a few more years due to family responsibilities — her husband, who was one of her clients, abandoned the family years ago — Savitri eventually quit. Now, about 10 years later, her elder daughter works with an NGO and is preparing to write the police exam, while her younger daughter is preparing for medical entrance tests in Indore.
The family belongs to the Banchhada community, a de-notified tribe with an estimated population of 25,000 spread across 78 villages in the districts of Mandsaur, Neemuch, and Ratlam in western Madhya Pradesh.
Unlike Savitri’s daughters, most girls in the community are born into a system in which their families expect them to enter sex work — a practice passed down over generations. According to several members of the community and NGOs in the region, while many Indians celebrate the birth of a boy over a girl, the Banchhadas welcome a girl with sweets and firecrackers. As girls grow up, they receive better nutrition than boys. They are given expensive clothes and, unlike in much of India, are not told that they will have to marry one day and leave the nest.
The reason, however, is disturbing: for generations, the Banchhada girls have been pushed into sex work upon hitting puberty and given the responsibility of earning. Their family members function as pimps and live off their money.
Akash Chouhan, founder of the Jan Shaurya Social Welfare and Development Society, an NGO based in Neemuch, estimates that at least 10,000 women of the community, including about 3,000 girls, remain trapped in this form of exploitation. “Girls are forced to drop out of school after Class 8 or 9 and are pushed into sex work by their families,” says Akash, who is from the community. “Community elders protect the practice in the name of tradition.”
Radhika, a sex worker, says girls are conditioned from childhood to believe in the tradition. They are told it is their responsibility to ease the family’s financial woes. “I quit school on my own after Class 9 and began working,” she says. “But if a girl refuses to quit, her family forces her into sex work through physical or emotional abuse.”
Abuse along the highway
A drive along State Highway 156, which connects the three districts, passes through several villages of the community. Girls wearing bright lipstick stand along the way, while older women sit on cots outside their houses and shanties, watching children playing nearby. As evening approaches, they gesture to men to come in.
In Neemuch’s Jaitpura village, an elderly woman approaches a car parked on the roadside and asks if anyone would like to come in. She points to three girls sitting outside her house; two of them are her granddaughters. “You can pick either of them and go into the house,” she tells them. “It will cost you ₹300 for 10 minutes, but I will take ₹100 as my tip. The room has a fan; you will be comfortable.”
Most girls along the highway, including those who look underage, say that they are around 20; some say they recently turned 18. Conversations with them reveal that they have been involved in sex work for about four years.
Multiple dhabas along the highway are also involved in brokering deals between prospective clients and sex workers. The owner of a highway dhaba in Ratlam’s Dhodar village claims he can “arrange girls” and lists different price brackets based on location, duration, and the girl’s age. Standing near a toll booth, he lists the facilities available, including an air-conditioned room, car parking, and assurances of safety from the police. The rates range from ₹300 for 10 minutes to ₹1,000 for an hour, and ₹6,000 for a night. They go up to ₹10,000 for a younger girl.
“If girls are taken to a hotel, clients face the risk of police raids. But here, clients have no problem,” the dhaba owner explains. “The girls avoid going to hotels as they face incidents of violence by drunken men. That is why many of them have built rooms in their houses with AC.”
Several sex workers from the region also travel to cities such as Indore in Madhya Pradesh and Chittorgarh and Udaipur in neighbouring Rajasthan, on client requests.
Shivangi, a former sex worker in Neemuch’s Nilkanthpura, who now works with the government’s Women and Child Development (WCD) Department, recalls some of the horrific incidents she faced. “In 2003, my friend and I had gone to a hotel in Chittorgarh for two clients. After a few minutes, two or three others entered the room. For hours, we suffered sexual and physical violence that still haunts me. All I could think of was jumping out a window,” says Shivangi, who is now married with two daughters.
Shivangi says girls rarely share grim experiences with their families as they have to “get to work as soon as the next client approaches”.
In 2005, Shivangi came in contact with an international NGO working in the region and began volunteering with it while continuing sex work. “Over the next few years, my mindset began to change as I got exposed to a life outside my community,” she says. “In 2008, I chose to leave that life behind for good. I married a man I met during my NGO work and moved in with him.”
From a criminal tribe to social outcasts
Historically a nomadic community in the Malwa and Mewar regions of present-day Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, the Banchhada community was notified as a ‘criminal tribe’ by the British government under the Criminal Tribes Act, 1871.
Narendra Chouhan, founder of Naya Jeevan Foundation, an NGO working for the youth of the community, says the origin of sex work in the community can be traced back to that period. “Our elders have told us that it began during the British Raj, when the police would catch men from the community and demand women in exchange for their release. Some families who could not pay money started sending them unmarried girls from their homes,” he says.
The community was de-notified by the Government of India in 1952 and classified as a Scheduled Caste. The practice that ensured monetary benefits for families continued, says Narendra. “Slowly, families who were engaged in sex work started moving out of Rajasthan and settled in this region.”
Apart from offering services in their homes, they also began offering services in trucks. A girl would board a truck at one location, offer services, and get off at another. “This method went on till the 2010s when people started buying land along the highway and building houses,” he says.
Barriers to a better life
Today, the Banchhadas remain cut off from mainstream society, with their members facing stigma in all walks of life: from education to employment to renting properties in cities. In many villages with a mixed population, the houses of the Banchhadas remain secluded. In Hadi Pipliya, for instance, the two sections are divided by a drain.
Kanupriya, a counsellor with Jan Shaurya, says members of the community, including women who are not involved in sex work, face job rejections in the private sector as soon as they reveal their social identity. “I have been rejected from various jobs myself,” she says. “Schools often deny admissions to Banchhada children. They say taking them in could disturb the atmosphere of their institution.”
Aditi Garg, who was Mandsaur Collector until recently, says the administration is trying its best to bridge the gap. Once, when the administration had recommended some women from the community, living in a government hostel, for teaching and teaching assistant jobs at private schools, there was pushback, she recalls. “The managements were concerned about their reputation, but we dealt with them firmly and ensured jobs for 24 women from the community. We have also hired some women on help desks in government offices where the public has to communicate with them,” she says.
The youth of the community find it hard to obtain government documents, especially a caste certificate, since many of them are born out of wedlock and have no records of their fathers. The absence of a caste certificate means that they are deprived of various government benefits such as reservation and scholarships.
Neemuch Collector Himanshu Chandra says the district administration has written to the government seeking a provision to help the community. “This is a policy problem. Since a person’s caste is decided based on the father’s caste, we can’t do much at our end,” he says.
Narendra says it is because of these reasons that many girls who want to leave sex work stay trapped. “They see no scope outside this profession. Some of those who did manage to escape or were rescued returned to sex work,” he says.
A government official adds that some girls who were rescued and rehabilitated at government hostels and centres returned to sex work as they had to vacate these places on turning 18. “While the government is running initiatives and programmes to provide them livelihood options such as sewing or skill-based jobs, it is difficult to match the income and lifestyle the girls earn through sex work. This leaves a gap in our efforts to rehabilitate the community,” the official adds.
In Mandsaur, however, Ms. Garg says the district administration has been able to find a way to issue caste certificates through ancestral records or any fraternal records that can establish a person’s connection to their family.
A cycle of exploitation
A recent short film, Khilawadi, which has received awards at various national and international film festivals, depicts the story of a Banchhada girl who dreams of becoming a doctor. Made by a debutant filmmaker, Shobhita Thakur, the film’s title comes from a local term often used for the oldest daughter of a family, who is not allowed to have a life of her own, whether it is a career or marriage.
In the Banchhada community, dowry is paid by the groom’s family to the bride’s. The reason is simple: her in-laws compensate her family for lost income. Activists and community members say the amount has increased over the years, with some girls’ families even taking ₹25 lakh.
As per the community’s customs, a girl cannot marry within the caste once she enters sex work. A married woman is not allowed into sex work.
Sangita, a social worker with Udan Women Employment Welfare Society, explains that the girls are fed ideas against marriage from childhood and encouraged to get into sex work, which promises materialistic benefits such as smartphones, scooters, and clothes. “They tell the girl that if she is unmarried, she can buy whatever she wants, but if she gets married, she will be stuck doing household chores,” says Sangita.
After the age of 25, many women are forced to become brokers or offer their houses on commission as client demand begins to decline. Others, suffering from infections, sexually transmitted diseases, or HIV/AIDS, become dependent on relatives or NGOs.
While researching for her film, Shobhita found that a girl suffering from AIDS was in the hospital. “The girl’s father came to the hospital in a drunken state and asked her to give him money even though she was in a critical condition. He created a scene and left. The girl died a few days later.” She says she came across many incidents that were so revolting that she could not include them in the film.
Sex workers say it is because demand goes down with age that they take on as many clients as they can. Radhika says she has about 10-15 clients a day and earns about ₹5,000. “I don’t have a large family; I only have my grandmother. So, I have to save enough to buy a house and live comfortably after a few years,” she reasons.
Sangita says the girls are unable to escape as caste panchayats punish or penalise those who try to break free from the practice. She adds that the community has an unofficial nexus of pimps and agents that keeps a close watch on the girls, including those who have been rescued.
Ms. Garg adds that caste panchayats and community members oppose programmes they believe could affect the profession. “We recently faced resistance during our HPV [human papillomavirus vaccination] drive for cervical cancer as they feared it could impact their girls’ work,” she says.
A generation of hope
Social activists allege that multiple government campaigns and programmes have failed to impact the community.
For instance, the Jabali Scheme launched by the State government remains “completely missing from the ground,” Akash says. Launched in the early 1990s, it was aimed at building hostels for the women from the Banchhada and Bedia communities that are involved in caste-based sex work. Officials say there has been no allocation for the scheme for about four years. “Even when it was active, the allocation was just about ₹5 lakh-7 lakh a year for a district,” says a WCD official.
Narendra says most government programmes focus on creating awareness instead of providing women with alternative livelihood options and erasing the stigma. “And even their awareness drives often turn into photo opportunities for government officials,” he points out.
Meanwhile, NGOs have been running learning centres for children of the community so that they can resist their families’ push when the time comes. The youth in various villages also have initiatives to do away with the practice.
In Sagargram, a group of mostly college-going youth formed a committee about four years ago. Within a year, they were able to stop sex work and liquor inside their village. “We faced objections, but we stood our ground,” says Vikas Chouhan, a Master of Social Work student.
Saniya, who is part of the committee, says she encouraged a friend, who was being pressured by her family to get into sex work, to fight back. “Her parents came to my house to complain to my parents, but my parents took my side. My friend fought with her parents, and they eventually relented. She is now continuing her studies,” she says.
Her approach was simple, Saniya explains. “Start with one house, one person, then move up. Now, our village feels much safer,” she says.
mehul.malpani@thehindu.co.in

title: Domestic violence victim left traumatised after Travelodge staff gave abuser room key
content:
Domestic violence victim left traumatised after Travelodge staff gave abuser room key
Travelodge said they have since made immediate changes to its room access security policy
- Bookmark
A woman said she experienced one of the most “traumatic nights” of her life when she was attacked in her Travelodge hotel room after reception staff handed her abuser a key.
The domestic violence victim, who has not been named, told the BBC she was staying at a Travelodge in London in October last year when she was attacked in her room.
She contacted the broadcaster when she heard about the sentencing of a man who attacked a woman at a Travelodge in Maidenhead, Berkshire, in December 2022 after being given a key to her room. Kyran Smith was jailed for seven-and-a-half years in February.
The domestic violence victim told the BBC she had booked a room at the hotel for a “night away from the fear” after a period of abuse.
But her attacker was reportedly given access by reception staff.
The woman said of her abuser: “He walked into the hotel and told the receptionist that his girlfriend was upstairs having a seizure.
“He asked what room I was in and what floor I was staying on.”
Staff handed him a key and directed him to her room, she added.
Once inside, he physically attacked her and tried to grab her phone, the woman said.
She managed to convince him to leave, but he returned and became more aggressive.
“Not long afterwards, I heard him knocking at the door. He was banging, shouting. He was just getting more and more aggressive,” she said.
“I was terrified. I was hoping that he was going to stop, but instead, he kicked the hotel room door completely off the hinges.”
The woman said she went downstairs “shaking” and “begging for help”.
She added: “I think the receptionist just panicked. She didn’t call the police. She didn’t check if I needed any medical attention.
“She didn’t ask if there were any family members I could call, anyone that I needed.
“She just offered me a room, another room in the hotel.”
A Travelodge spokesperson said: “We are deeply sorry for the significant distress experienced by the customer and we apologise for the way the incident has been handled.
“Customer safety and security is – and remains – a priority for us.
“Any case of an unauthorised person entering a guest’s room is a significant cause for concern and we want to be clear that this should not have happened. Our room access security policies at the time were not correctly followed, which is not acceptable.
“Earlier this year, we made changes to strengthen our room access security policy and incident escalation procedures, supported by training for all of our customer-facing colleagues.”
Travelodge chief executive Jo Boydell previously said immediate changes were made to its room access security policy after Smith was sentenced for the 2022 attack.
In line with the changes, explicit permission is now required from guests before additional or replacement keys are issued for their room.
It builds on Travelodge’s existing policy to never confirm to a third party that a guest is staying at one of its hotels.
The national domestic abuse helpline offers support for women on 0808 2000 247, or you can visit the Refuge website. There is a dedicated men's advice line on 0808 8010 327. Those in the US can call the domestic violence hotline on 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). Other international helplines can be found via www.befrienders.org

title: Parents of baby girl killed at nursery fear unsafe sleeping ‘rife’ in sector across England
content:
The parents of a nine-month-old girl who died after being placed in an unsafe sleeping position at nursery said they feared poor practice may be “rife” across England.
Genevieve Meehan suffocated when she was strapped face down to a beanbag for an hour and 37 minutes at a nursery in Cheadle Hulme, Stockport, in May 2022.
Kate Roughley, the nursery’s deputy manager, was jailed for 14 years in 2024 after being found guilty of manslaughter. One of Roughley’s colleagues was later jailed for the “deplorable” treatment of other babies in her care.
Genevieve’s parents, Katie and John Meehan, have led a campaign with the charity the Lullaby Trust to strengthen safety and regulation of nurseries after a series of high-profile abuses.
The sector has come under intense scrutiny in recent months after the cases of Vincent Chan and Nathan Bennett, nursery workers who sexually assaulted children in their care.
Chan was jailed in February for 18 years for molesting young children in a campaign of sexual abuse that was described as “every parent’s worst nightmare”, while Bennett was jailed in March for 24 years for raping and abusing young children in his care.
Another nursery worker, Kimberley Cookson, was jailed in April over the death of 14-month-old Noah Sibanda, who had been physically restrained face-down with a blanket over his head while being put to sleep.
As a result of Genevieve’s parents’ campaign, childcare settings in England will be banned from September from putting babies under 12 months to sleep in anything other than a cot.
Ofsted, the regulator, will triple the number of unannounced inspections – adding an extra 3,000 visits a year, boosted by an additional £8m from the government – and inspect nurseries every four years instead of six. Each visit will scrutinise sleeping policies.
Katie Meehan, 42, said she was “really shocked” by the extent of unsafe sleeping practice that had been revealed when nurseries wrote privately to the government about the planned changes this year.
Some reported leaving babies to sleep in pushchairs “due to space limitations”, according to details shared with the Department for Education (DfE). Others put infants to sleep outside, adopting “forest school models or Scandinavian practices”.
By law, nurseries are required to follow NHS safer sleep guidance – which includes laying the baby on their back in a cot or Moses basket – however, in the rules from September, the government will state: “Babies aged one year and under must only be placed to sleep in a cot.”
Katie Meehan, who is working closely with the government and Ofsted, said the responses suggested unsafe sleeping may be “rife” across England and that they were a “wake-up call” for the regulator and officials.
Some nursery owners said they would be forced to reduce the number of infants they take as a result of the new rules. Several raised concerns that this will ban smaller beds, such as dream coracles, which take up less space than a cot and have been widely adopted in recent years.
John Meehan, 40, said he was concerned some nursery owners – many of whom are backed by private equity firms – were potentially putting profit before safety.
“There are lots and lots of people out there who just want to do their absolute best and they go into that industry because they want to look after children,” he said. “But my impression from some of the responses is that they are taking too many children and there is a money incentive for them to do so, and that is a real concern.”
Ministers are now considering whether to introduce mandatory CCTV to all nurseries in England, one of the key aims of the campaign. Olivia Bailey, the former early years minister who spearheaded the latest reforms, is understood to have been very persuaded by the arguments for mandatory CCTV.
Katie Meehan said she was disappointed that Bailey lost her role in the reshuffle when Andy Burnham became prime minister. However, she is hopeful Burnham will take up the reforms, having met Genevieve’s family this year when he was mayor of Greater Manchester.
She said Burnham was particularly supportive of their call for mandatory CCTV – which was crucial in securing Genevieve’s killer’s conviction – and that he had told them: “Genevieve was a child of Manchester and she was failed. We’ve got to make sure it doesn’t happen again.”
The DfE said: “What happened to Genevieve was a tragedy, and her parents’ campaigning has already changed practice across the country. We will keep going until no family goes through what theirs has.
“The vast majority of settings do a brilliant job, and the response to our updated guidance showed a sector that wants to get this right. But settings have long been legally required to follow NHS safer sleep guidance, and that is why we are working with the Lullaby Trust to make those expectations unambiguous, so there can be no excuses for unsafe practice.”
Sir Martyn Oliver, the chief inspector at Ofsted, said: “No parent should have to endure what Katie and John have been through. They have shown remarkable bravery in pursuing change following their daughter’s tragic death.
“We welcome the DfE’s additional funding for more frequent inspections, including thousands more without notice visits. We’re also strengthening our inspection practice so that safe sleeping in nurseries and with childminders is now a mandatory part of every inspection and will be reported on for parents to read.”

title: Assault, harassment and stalking top calls to victim line
content:
Almost one in every two crime-related contacts received by Ireland's national victims' support service last year related to assault, harassment or stalking.
The Crime Victims Helpline (CVH) supported 5,902 contacts in 2025, and provided 3,268 referrals to specialist victim support, criminal justice and community services.
Founded just over 20 years ago, the helpline provides information and support to victims of crime in Ireland.
The number of contacts supported by the charity last year fell by almost 1,000 contacts (967) compared to the previous year.
Its latest annual report shows that assault accounted for 24% of recorded crime-related contacts, while harassment and stalking accounted for a further 21%.
Fraud was the third most common crime type and figures also show that hate-motivated crimes increased year-on-year over the past ten years.
While official crime statistics record offences, the CVH report captures the human impact of crime.
In 2025, the helpline signposted people to a wide range of statutory, specialist and community-based services.
The majority of referrals related to gardaí, garda victim service offices and criminal justice processes.
It connected people with counselling and mental health supports, legal information, fraud and cybercrime supports, domestic abuse and sexual violence services, housing and practical supports, migrant and minority ethnic community organisations, older person and disability advocacy services, and other specialist victim support services.
Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan commended the Crime Victims Helpline for playing "a vital role" in providing access to a trusted source of information and support including specialist statutory and community-based services.
He described the latest annual report as "a valuable snapshot of the experiences of people impacted by crime and of the important role the helpline plays in meeting the need for information, support, and guidance".
Chief Executive of Crime Victims Helpline Michele Puckhaber said no one should have to face the impact of crime in isolation.
"Whether someone needs information about the justice system, emotional support or help accessing specialist services, our message is simple: support is available, and you do not have to go through it alone," Ms Puckhaber said.
